newsitem.title: UK: Investors asking if emerging market rally is over.
newsitem.headline: Investors asking if emerging market rally is over.

text.p: Investors will be looking this week for signs whether the January emerging market rally is starting to flag, assessing where to take profits and where to hold on for continued upward momentum, strategists say.
Turkey and Russia will top the agenda with equity market investors hungry for a slice of the Turkish action but weighing profit-taking in Russia, they said.

"We've got to see whether (the rally) lasts past February," said one analyst at a major U.S. investment firm here, referring to the inflows of fresh U.S. mutual fund cash currently fuelling steep emerging stock market rises.
"Mid-February is when the new money usually runs out."

TURKEY, the best performer over the year to date after rising 35 percent on the IFC emerging market index, will not be first to ease. It got a filip last week from good news on privatisation and a budget deficit better than officials or the markets had predicted.

"The Turkish courts have finally allowed the privatisation of Turkish Telekom to go ahead...and the budget deficit has turned out better than the markets expected," said HSBC James Capel emerging market strategist Nigel Rendell.
On Monday morning the Turkish stock market index jumped 7.32 percent in early trade.
Turkish courts had blocked moves to privatise the utility several times before they assented last week, sending its stock market higher. Analysts see continued buoyancy this week.
"It's probably worth $3.5 billion in terms of revenue for the government, so the fiscal side has improved overnight," Rendell added, referring to the impact of the Telekom privatisation plans.

RUSSIA too will continue to preoccupy investors after the Duma last week debated a motion on trying to oust President Boris Yeltsin because of ill health. Deliberations continue next month and market will be jittery in the run up.

"Although the Duma has no constitutional ability to oust Yeltsin, this will seriously undermine the authority of the president," HSBC's Rendell said, adding key players would be jostling in earnest for position.
"Russia has gone up 42 percent in dollar terms (this year), so it may be ready for some profit-taking," he added.

Like Turkey, HUNGARY too has attracted investor enthusiasm, last year's heady stock market performance continuing with a 22 percent rise so far in 1997, amid positive sentiment that shows no sign of abating.
But trouble persists elsewhere in the Balkans.
BULGARIA's central bank warned on Friday it lacked the resources to control the country's deepening economic crisis, compounded by ongoing political deadlock.
Investors have been steering clear for weeks, nervous as a January 28 deadline approaches for the payment of the interest coupons on its outstanding Brady debt.
Although the government has indicated it will not default, concerns have not been totally allayed, and investors are already anxiously eyeing the July instalment.
Thousands of protestors marched through the capital on Sunday, demanding a general election but the ruling Socialist party repeated its insistence on forming a new cabinet.
And in SERBIA 10 weeks of pro-democracy protests continued as more than 300,000 people filed through central Belgrade on Monday.
Investors say the chance of a deal restructuring Serbia's debt are receding daily.
Investors meanwhile are flocking to LATVIA after Standard & Poor's awarded it the coveted investment grade credit rating, making it the first Baltic nation to win the accolade.
Foreign banks snapped up the government's latest Treasury bill issue on Friday, leaving little scope for local buyers.
In Latin America BRAZIL gears up for the first lower house vote, scheduled for this week, on a constitutional amendment to allow President Fernando Henrique Cardoso to stand for a second term.

Delays insisted upon by officials from Congress's biggest party may mean the government may face a tougher than expected ride, though the local market has priced approval in and foreign investors have increasingly followed suit.

Brazilian stocks last week shrugged off negative news of December's hefty trade deficit, and news that privatisation of mining giant CVRD had been postponed to April from the first quarter of this year.

After powering ahead since the start of the year, COLOMBIA's equity market suffered a reversal last week on growing fears of U.S. decertification in March, after two of the most prominent Cali drug cartel members received comparatively light sentences.
Threats of a public sector strike for 11 February will compound the downturn, promoting a bearish market tone in the near term, strategists say.
Foreign & Colonial said new tax measures, plus planned cuts in government expenditure, had raised fears of lower than anticipated economic growth for 1997.
Export firms in CHILE meanwhile may continue to suffer in the week ahead after last week's modification to the country's exchange rate mechanism, which has boosted the peso's strength.
The IFC emerging market composite investable index, IFC/IPRD, denominated in dollars, rose 0.9 percent week-on-week to 1,225 points on Friday compared with a week earlier.
Latin America was up 0.5 percent week-on-week at 587.16, Asia was up 0.9 percent at 262.13, and Europe, Middle East and Africa were up 1.0 percent at 145.37.
